# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

- jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc allocator) lowered 99th-percentile latency of kestrel (our key-value store) by 59%.
- Throughput and median latency stayed within run-to-run variation in this read-mostly test.
- The 5.7 GB (9.3%) rise in memory use needs approval from the capacity team.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store, the program under test.
- **jemalloc**: the memory allocator that kestrel uses today.
- **jf2**: our fork of jemalloc.
- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa of the main branch, with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit, with jf2 in place of jemalloc 5.3.
- **YCSB**: a standard benchmark for key-value stores. YCSB-B is its read-mostly workload. YCSB-A is its write-heavy workload.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. For example, 99% of requests finish within the p99 latency.
- **Spike**: a short period of high latency.
- **Spread**: the highest run minus the lowest run.
- **Decay purge**: the allocator step that returns unused memory to the operating system.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory that the process uses.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **perf**: the Linux sampling profiler.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding the process to the cores and memory of one processor socket.

## Test setup

- Goal: check if jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.
- Host: bench-07 (the test server) has 2 x 32-core Xeon processors and 512 GB of memory. It runs Linux kernel 6.8.
- System load: the load average before the runs was 0.4 (less than one busy core of 64).
- Workload: YCSB-B with 64 client threads.
- Runs: 5 runs per build, 10 minutes each, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, ...).
- Reported values: the median of the 5 runs, with the lowest and highest run in parentheses.

## Results

```
p99 and p99.9 latency, median of 5 runs. 1 block = 200 us.

p99    A  ███████████ 2140 us
       B  ████ 870 us                    59% lower

p99.9  A  █████████████████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B  ████████████████ 3100 us       68% lower
```

Only p99 and p99.9 changed. Throughput and p50 stayed within the spread between runs.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change, B against A |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput (kops/s) | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -0.7%, ranges overlap |
| p50 latency (us) | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +0.8%, ranges overlap |
| p99 latency (us) | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -59%, ranges do not overlap |
| p99.9 latency (us) | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -68%, ranges do not overlap |
| RSS at end of run (GB) | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 GB (+9.3%) |

- **p99 latency**: B is 59% lower. The highest B run (940 us) is below the lowest A run (1890 us) [Ref1].
- **p99.9 latency**: B is 68% lower. The highest B run (3900 us) is below the lowest A run (7200 us) [Ref1].
- **Throughput**: B is 3 kops/s (0.7%) lower. This difference is smaller than the 13 kops/s spread of the A runs [Ref1].
- **p50 latency**: B is 1 us (0.8%) higher. This difference is smaller than the 5 us spread of the A runs [Ref1].
- **RSS**: B uses 5.7 GB (9.3%) more memory at the end of a run. No run-to-run range was recorded for RSS [Ref1].

## Likely cause of the spikes

- Observation: the spikes in build A occur at the same times as the jemalloc decay purge [Ref2].
- Evidence: 31% of the perf samples taken during the spikes are in `je_arena_decay` (the jemalloc purge function) [Ref2].
- Difference in build B: jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- Hypothesis: moving the purge to a background thread is the cause of the lower p99 and p99.9. A perf profile of build B was not taken. Such a profile would confirm or reject the hypothesis.

## One run was replaced

- Event: run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7.
- Cause: the stall was traced to logrotate (the system log rotation job). The nightly cron job (a scheduled system task) started it. The allocator was not the cause [Ref3].
- Action: run 3 was repeated. The B results above use the repeated run.

## Not tested

Insufficient data for the three cases below. The results above apply only to YCSB-B with 64 client threads and no NUMA pinning.

- Write-heavy workload (YCSB-A): the run planned for tomorrow resolves this.
- More than 64 client threads: a run with a higher thread count resolves this.
- NUMA pinning: a run with pinning enabled resolves this.

## Open decision

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must answer this.

## Next steps

1. Run YCSB-A on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment) with a feature flag (an on/off switch).

## References

- [Ref1] Results table in this report. Source: 5 runs per build on bench-07, 2026-11-20.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A during the spikes, same test session.
- [Ref3] Test notes on build B run 3 and its repeat, same test session.

---

**Points to check before you send it**

- Step 3 condition: your notes say "if ok". I read that as the capacity team's approval only. Change step 3 if the YCSB-A result is also a condition.
- Hypothesis label: your notes hold no perf profile of build B. So I marked the background-thread explanation as a hypothesis. Remove the label if you have that profile.
- Values I derived from your medians and ranges:
  - latency reductions: 59% and 68%
  - throughput and p50 changes: 0.7% and 0.8%
  - spreads of the A runs: 13 kops/s and 5 us
- YCSB-B description: "read-mostly" comes from the public YCSB definition, not from your notes.
- Not in your notes: the nightly logrotate job can also disturb tomorrow's YCSB-A run.
